speaker: SPEAKER_01
transcript: This is Wally Knox. Welcome to the Political Conversation. I'm always surprised after a hard fought election that Congress is still in session with exactly the same crew as before the election. of the defeated members of Congress are gone. They're still there, and none of the newly elected folks have joined. That's because there's no change in Congress until January the 3rd. It's called a lame duck session, and it's called that because a lame duck and a group of ducks is picked off by the local fox, and defeated members of Congress are the political lame ducks. This lame duck session has a host of important legislation coming before it, including authorization bills for the Defense Department and for overall government operations, as well as the Respect for Marriage bill protecting same-sex and interracial marriages. Another major issue to be dealt with in the lame duck session is one meant to prevent a replay of January 6, 2021, in which challenges to some electoral college delegations could have overturned the actual results of the election and precipitated a true constitutional crisis. This is called the Electoral Count Act issue. Earlier this year, I spoke to Congressman Adam Schiff about the prospects of passing a reform of the Electoral Count Act. Let's listen to what we said in that conversation.

transcript: I think Adam's early optimism about the reform of the Electoral Count Act was right on point. There is now great optimism about passage of the reform. There are now two versions of the bill, a House version which was authored by Democrat Zollofgren and the Senate version authored by Republican Senator Susan Collins. The version we discussed earlier with the author of Angus King has been passed over in favor of the Collins bill in the Senate. That bill now has 36 co-sponsors, including 15 Republican senators not counting Collins. One of these Republican co-sponsors is Mitch McConnell, the Republican leader in the Senate. So the bill has more than enough Republican co-sponsors to overcome a filibuster and will certainly make it to a final vote. Which of these versions will prevail, the House or the Senate version? My own view is that this is an area of the law, how the President is finally selected, in which having a bipartisan backing is very essential. And the fact that the Senate's version is authored by Republican Susan Collins is a significant advantage in and of itself. Imagine if the law that defines how the president is selected was determined by Democrats alone. I can hear someone we all know very well saying it's rigged. But there's another reason why the Senate bill will prevail. It's the Senate filibuster. The House version will never be able to surmount the filibuster in the face of the Collinsville sitting there. No Republican has a reason to support it. In contrast, the Collins bill will fly. There's an additional reason why Republicans will support this. The fact that the sitting vice president is Kamala Harris gives Republicans a real reason for reform. If the Republicans win the 2024 election, they don't want Harris to balk at the official count. On top of that, when they explain their supportive reform, they can always say, and I am sure they will, that they did it specifically to take power away from Harris. The fact that so many Republicans, including McConnell, have signed on to Collins bill, leads me to think they've crossed the Rubicon on the issue, and there is literally no turning back for them. All of them will pay some political price for cosponsoring the bill. And none of them wants to pay that price and yet get no policy improvement in exchange. In short, I think it's over except for the official casting of votes. And here's my count on that. If all Democrats vote for it and the only Republican cosponsors are those Republicans who vote for it, The bill will sail through in a bipartisan 66-34 vote. But if the bill's in such good shape, why wasn't it brought up immediately after the November elections? Why not before today, December the 6th? Here's my take. Because Chuck Schumer did not want Raphael Warnock casting a vote on the bill before his runoff election, it's just too darn inflammatory. They want to give Warnock every possible opportunity to win his election, which is being conducted today. The Democrats are being strategic. But now they have to move ahead rapidly. There are very few days left to deal with the issue. The calendar of meetings for the House has just six meeting days left after today before the new House takes over. Before December 6th, it could not be brought up. After December the 6th, it has to move quickly. Turning to my coming political conversations, there's widespread agreement that independence made the crucial decisions in many of the 2022 elections. So we will revisit my conversation with Samara Klar of the University of Arizona to discuss just who are the independents. And then I'll talk to a series of sharp observers about the 2022 results. Morris Fiorena of Stanford, an author of Unstable Majorities, will join us once again. Joan Williams, author of White Working Class, and Lynn Vaverick, UCLA professor and author of The Bitter and Will Also Way In. I want to thank, once again, Congressman Adam Schiff, and I want to thank, once again, my producer and a kumu for her excellent work. Looking forward to seeing you next time on the Political Conversation.
